header: Date: 2026-12-29 14:30 UTC; Duration: 46m; Attendees: Redwood AE + SE, Avalon AI CTO/Platform/SRE/Data Science
summary: Discovery focused on streaming p95 latency and aggregate tokens/sec throughput. Avalon wants <300ms p95 for short, interactive responses, and a plan for sustained concurrency ~150 with bursts to 500. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, benchmarks to run, SOC2/KMS questions, and next steps to run a 2-hour spike test.
transcript:
[00:00] Aisha: Hey everybody, thanks for joining — we really appreciate you making time. Quick intros?
[00:10] Lena: Hi all, Lena Ortiz, CTO at Avalon. We've got Markus, Priya and Tom on the call.
[00:14] Markus: Hey. Markus V. platform team.
[00:17] Priya: Priya, SRE, hi.
[00:19] Tom: Tom, data science.
[00:21] Ethan: Ethan Park, SE from Redwood — I'll be hands-on for the perf bits.
[00:25] Aisha: Cool. Goal for today is to understand your latency & throughput targets, current infra, and any compliance constraints. We'll then map hosted/dedicated/private options.
[00:36] Lena: Right, to kick off — top level: we run interactive chat agent for customers, median response size is small, like 20-60 tokens, but we also have longer generation jobs up to 1k tokens for reports. We care about p95 for the short flows because that's UX-critical. We're targeting ideally under 300ms p95 for short responses, with concurrency around 150 sustained and bursts to 500.
[00:58] Ethan: Understood. When you say p95 <300ms for short responses, that's end-to-end including your app + network, or just model inference?
[01:05] Lena: Ideally end-to-end, but we know network adds some. For planning assume 250ms model side p95 to reach ~300ms for user.
[01:13] Markus: Also, streaming is important — we stream tokens to the client as they arrive. That changes how we think about per-token latency versus full-response latency.
[01:22] Aisha: Good point. We'll need to separate per-token tail latency (p95/p99 of first token) vs time-to-first-byte and token throughput.
[01:30] Tom: For token/sec, one of our questions — is that token/sec per model instance, or aggregated? We want to know how to size capacity for 2k-5k tokens/sec aggregate during business hours.
[01:40] Ethan: Typically we measure both: tokens/sec per GPU (or vCPU config) and aggregate capacity across Redwood pools. For hosted we give expected profiles per model; for Dedicated you get predictable throughput and can cap concurrency.
[01:53] Priya: Security: we are regulated in EU and must have KMS-managed keys plus audit logs for all inference calls. Also SOC2 is a requirement.
[02:02] Marta: Short answer — Redwood has SOC2 and offers KMS integrations, VPC options for Private deployments, and full audit logs in the Console. We'll share the certs.
[02:11] Lena: Great. There's also a cost question — do we go hosted or Dedicated? We need to see unit economics at our scale.
[02:18] Aisha: Totally. We usually do a benchmark run with your representative prompts. We recommend a two-tier test: one focused on p95 tail for interactive short prompts (bursty concurrency) and one sustained throughput test for longer jobs.
[02:33] Markus: What about streaming p95 measurement? Is that per-token p95 or per-chunk?
[02:38] Ethan: We typically measure time-to-first-token p95 and per-token add latency p95. For streaming UX you care about time-to-first-token (TTFT) and steady-state token rate (tokens/sec). If TTFT is 200ms and tokens/sec is 20, that's a good interactive feel.
[02:53] Tom: 20 tokens/sec is on the low side for some of our models — we see 10-30 tokens/sec depending on model size.
[03:00] Aisha: Right. Also quantization and kernel selection affect steady token/sec. For larger 70B models you'll see lower token/sec per GPU than for 7B.
[03:08] Markus: Our current infra is a mix: we run some internal smaller models on Triton, but main thing is our services call external APIs for the big models. Latency is variable, plus we don't have a good autoscaling profile for burst spikes.
[03:20] Priya: And we need to guarantee that spikes up to 500 concurrent streams don't cause cascading failures in our API layer. So any solution needs decent burst capacity or a fallback plan.
[03:32] Ethan: Two things we can do: Dedicated with reserved pools and burst capacity configured, or Hosted with cross-region capacity and smart routing. Both support automatic fallback to smaller model variants if needed.
[03:43] Lena: How predictable are p95 numbers in Hosted? We need an SLA-ish expectation for p95 during business hours.
[03:50] Marta: Hosted has published perf profiles per model; we can give you 95th percentiles under typical load and also run a dedicated spike test. For contractual SLAs, Dedicated or Private can be negotiated.
[04:03] Tom: Would you do a token/sec benchmark for our prompt suite?
[04:06] Ethan: Yes — we'll send a harness and a spreadsheet. We ask for 50-100 representative prompts, distribution of lengths, and request traces. We'll run token/sec and p95 sampling across model variants.
[04:20] Markus: Markus here — one nuance, our front-end expects chunked streaming every 150ms ideally; if tokens are slower, it looks jittery. Can Redwood guarantee small chunk intervals?
[04:31] Ethan: We can tune batching windows and the KV cache behavior to favor lower per-token latency. There's a tradeoff: smaller batching lowers throughput (more GPU cycles) and raises cost per token. We'll show numbers so you can pick a cost vs latency point.
[04:48] Lena: Also, is there an on-prem option? For some customers we must do on-prem in air-gapped sites.
[04:53] Marta: Yes, Redwood Private supports on-prem packages and VPC deployments with KMS/HSM support. For air-gapped there's a longer onboarding but it's supported.
[05:02] Aisha: Let's talk numbers — if you need 250ms model-side p95 for short prompts, for a 13B model we'd expect roughly X p95 on a single A100-like GPU? Sorry, Ethan — can you ballpark?
[05:13] Ethan: Ballpark: optimized runtime on A100-ish, for 13B you're often in the 40-120ms per token range for steady-state, but tail can push to ~200-300ms depending on sequence length and KV hit rates. For first token cold-starts can be higher unless KV cache is warm. For 70B models, per-token is notably higher, maybe 150-400ms steady.
[05:35] Tom: So to achieve 250ms p95 for our short 20-token responses, we'd need a model/version that keeps per-token latency low. Sounds like either smaller 13B or optimized 70B with quantization.
[05:45] Ethan: Exactly. And Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization and batching settings by workload. We'll include those recommendations in the follow-up.
[05:53] Markus: For aggregate tokens/sec — we want to size for 3k tokens/sec sustained across all users. How do we translate that into instances/pool size?
[06:02] Ethan: We'll run the math once we have your representative prompts. As a crude example: if a model instance does 100 tokens/sec steady, you'd need ~30 instances. But batch efficiency can improve tokens/sec with higher concurrency. We can show both conservative and optimistic sizing.
[06:17] Priya: How is KV cache handled in Hosted? We worry about cache warmness when routing across pools or regions.
[06:23] Marta: Hosted does automated prefix/KV caching, but there are cold-cache scenarios. For high cache locality, Dedicated or Private gives stronger guarantees since the same pool serves your traffic. We also have cache-aware routing.
[06:34] Lena: On SSO and audit — we need SAML SSO and detailed per-request logging for audits. Is that in Console?
[06:40] Aisha: Yes. SAML/SSO and RBAC are available. Audit logs with per-request metadata can be exported to your SIEM. We'll attach the docs.
[06:49] Tom: Any guidance on fallback strategies? If p95 spikes, how to degrade gracefully?
[06:54] Ethan: Common patterns: fallback to smaller model variant (fast but less capable), reduce max tokens or apply rate-limiting, or serve cached responses for common prompts. Redwood supports canary rollouts and automatic fallback policies.
[07:07] Markus: Ok. Can we talk about the planned spike test? We want a 2-hour window to simulate bursts up to 500 concurrent streams and measure p95 and tokens/sec.
[07:16] Aisha: Yes — we'll provision a spike window. We'll need your traffic script and expected prompt distribution. We'll also capture server-side metrics and token traces.
[07:25] Priya: For the spike we need guarantees that it won't affect other tenants. Will Hosted isolate our burst?
[07:31] Marta: In Hosted, bursts are handled by capacity pools; for strict isolation Dedicated is better. For the test we can allocate a controlled environment so you get reliable numbers.
[07:41] Lena: Cost sensitivity is critical — show us cost per 1M tokens at target p95.
[07:46] Aisha: We'll provide a cost model for Hosted vs Dedicated across your expected load and show break-even points.
[07:54] Tom: Quick question — do you support server-side streaming jitter smoothing? We see microbursts that lead to client glitches.
[07:59] Ethan: We can tune buffering and chunk aggregation on the server side. There's again a latency vs smoothness trade-off. We'll include recommended buffering parameters.
[08:09] Markus: If we go Dedicated, what are autoscale policies like? We need fast scale-up for small-duration bursts.
[08:16] Marta: Dedicated supports configurable autoscale with aggressive BU (burst up to reserved + burst capacity) and can pre-warm nodes. You can set policy thresholds by p95 or CPU/GPU queue depth.
[08:27] Lena: Any red flags we should watch for in the benchmark?
[08:31] Ethan: Watch for cold starts (first token high tail), batch window tuning causing token queuing, and cache misses. Also measure p95 across both short and long workflows — cost tradeoffs differ.
[08:44] Aisha: Okay, we'll summarize and capture next steps.
[08:48] [10:15] (cross-talk and short pause)
[10:30] Aisha: Recap — Redwood action: send benchmark harness, SOC2/ISO certs, Dedicated vs Hosted cost doc, and proposed 2-hour spike window on Jan 6. Avalon action: provide prompt sample set, request traces, and confirm regulatory constraints.
[10:49] Lena: Sounds good.
[10:51] Markus: One more — can you surface historical per-token cost numbers for sample models? That helps our finance team.
[10:57] Aisha: Yes, we'll include historical cost per million token estimates across model families.
[11:03] Priya: Great. Thanks all.
[11:06] Ethan: Thanks — we'll follow up in email with artifacts.
[11:10] Lena: Bye.
[11:12] [END]
